utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. The technicians and the interpreters are ready. All right. We shall resume our business today, and today for the Prosecution, we have Mr. Meddegoda?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Grant Niemann appears with me for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And for the Defence, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Goran Mikulicic and my colleague, Joka for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And the registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is the case IT-95-14/1-T, the Prosecution versus Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: All right. We have a witness today for the Defence, Mrs. Blazenka Vujica. Ms. Vujica, you will now make the solemn declaration which you have the text before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You may be seated. Thank you. Now you will answer the questions which Mr. Mikulicic will put to you. Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Vujica. I'm Goran Mikulicic, and with my colleague, Joka, I'm representing my client, Mr. Aleksovski and I shall ask you a few questions relating to this case and I should like to ask you to be so kind to answer them. Ms. Vujica, will you please tell us when and where were you were born?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: On the 6th of May, 1965, in Jazine, the municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Ms. Vujica, what is your ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you a practising believer?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, a Roman Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where did you receive education?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: At the secondary school centre in Vitez. I am an economic technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you attended that school in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: The elementary school in Vitez also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And now you live where?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Donje Polje, Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it a part of the town of Busovaca or is it a certain distance?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Three kilometres away from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Have you been living in Donje Polje always or have you moved there recently?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Some five years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Ms. Vujica, after you completed the secondary school and was trained as an economic technician, did you get a job somewhere?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, when I completed the secondary education I worked for a private store owner, shop owner who is my uncle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And that is your first job?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you worked for awhile for your uncle in his private shop. Did you find another employment or is it where you were when the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Sometime before the outbreak of the war, it was in -- I don't know, '92, 1992, in Bosnia, in Central Bosnia and Busovaca, nobody worked. That was a time when we all lost work. So that sometimes in mid December, '92, I was mobilised to the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So when the armed conflict commenced in Bosnia-Herzegovina as against the JNA, you lost your job like many other people in Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And then you say that in December 1992, you were mobilised for the military police?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Which army mobilised you?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujica, before you were mobilised for the military police of the HVO, did you have any experience with the military before that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No, no, mostly -- it was mostly men who were in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So this was your first encounter with the military organisation and military structure?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And where were you assigned to as a military policeman? What was your job?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: As a secretary, military policewoman secretary. I did both these things because in the military police, in the military police, women were not often taken into custody because women did not perpetrate offences like men, so that I also performed secretarial duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Please correct my if I'm wrong. I don't know if I understood you properly. You were a military policewoman first and to be responsible for women who, for some reason or the other, would come under the jurisdiction of the military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you were mobilised as a policewoman for women?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But you said that there were not many women taken into custody, that is, detained, so that you did not have to do it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: It is. I hardly ever did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So that was when you were assigned to a secretarial post?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. And where were you supposed to perform secretarial duties?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: For the military police. Well, in the meantime, the district military prison was established, and I was assigned by the military police to the district military prison. And then after I came there, I began to work immediately there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you properly, you were assigned to the district military prison at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was that the first encounter with facilities at Kaonik or have you visited them before that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No. Oh, you mean before the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I mean before the war?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No, no, nobody had access to the military facilities of the former JNA, women, in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. So you were posted on behalf -- by the military police to the district military prison in Kaonik and you were expected to perform secretarial duties there?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And when was it, roughly, when you first went to work in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember exactly, but I think it was somewhere around 15th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In comparison with your place of residence, how far was your job, that is, the military district prison of Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Seven or eight kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was there some organised urban transport so that you could go from your place of residence to your work place in district military prison in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No, at that time, we didn't have enough -- even enough fuel to use cars, so whatever other means of transportation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So how did you go to work?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Sometimes on foot, sometimes I would get a ride, hitchhike. It depended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what were your working hours?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: In the beginning, I worked mostly from 8 to 4 or from 7 to 3 -- no, I think it was from 8 to 4 as today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You say "as today." Does that mean that you still work for the same facility?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, six years in a row.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And is it still a prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, a district prison in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Right, but let us go back to the events of 1993. So you said your working hours were from 7 to 3 or from 8 to 4, that interval. Does that mean that in the afternoon hours or at night, you did not ever stay at the district military prison in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No, I had a small son so I could not stay and why should I stay? I mean, it wasn't my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And how old was your child?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: In '93, he was four years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Blazenka, prior to that, you had no experience with the military, you had no experience with work in a prison. So how did you learn what to do? How did you find out? Who showed you what your duties would be?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Well, at first, a policeman who was with the military police there, until the warden for the military prison in Busovaca, he showed me something too, although he never did anything like that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you came to the district prison, did you find there some military detainees? Do you remember who those people were? Do you know what was the status of those detainees and who had they been taken into custody by?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Criminal charges had been filed against some of them, and they were detained on the basis of orders of the district military court in Travnik, and others were serving punishment because of some disciplinary transgressions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you properly, there were two categories of detainees, one were those who were there serving with the basis of the rulings of the district military court in Travnik, and the second category were those who had committed some disciplinary offence and, therefore, were serving punishment upon the orders of their commanders, respective commanders. You mentioned the district military court in Travnik, Mrs. Vujica. Could you tell us the relationship between the district military court in Travnik and the district military prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: The district military court supervised -- it was the only one authorised to supervise the work of the district military prison in Busovaca, in relation to persons taken into custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if the president of the district military court ever came to visit the prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, he came in December, shortly after I came to the district military prison. He also came to pay a visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujica, do you remember, where were the guards recruited from, I mean, the guards who were on duty at the district military prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: From the military police, from Busovaca only.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So those guards were members of the military police just like you?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the beginning of the conflict in the territory of the municipality of Busovaca sometime in January '93?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when that was, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: The 25th, the 25th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Well, there was fire, shells were falling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you go to work that day?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No, not for the next five or six or maybe even ten days, because it was not safe. I did not dare because of my child.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And when the situation calmed down after some ten days or so, you could go back to work; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And when you came -- when you returned to work after that time, so it must have been the beginning of February, if I'm correct; is that so?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Whom did you find at the district military prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: The district military prison, in addition to detainees, subsequent to -- pursuant to their orders of the military district court and those on disciplinary punishment, there were some civilians who had been brought there presumably for their safety, because I told you there was fire rather fierce, and it was not safe, so that they were there, and I -- that was why I stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you meet, at that time, the warden of the military district prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What is his name?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you please indicate, if he is in this courtroom, if you see him?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, it is that gentleman over there. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For the record, the witness pointed in the direction of Mr. -- of the accused and identified him as Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski. So Mrs. Vujica, so it was then when you came to work some ten days after the conflict, you met Mr. Aleksovski for the first time?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did he introduce himself? Did he say who he was, what he was?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, he said, I'm Zlatko Aleksovski, the warden of the district military prison in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was he a member of your unit, the unit that you were also a member of, the military police?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No, no, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And from what he said, what he introduced himself, was he a member of some other military unit?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No. He was -- I think that he had been appointed by the ministry of justice. As a matter of fact, it was called then the department -- I can't remember, but it was the ministry of justice. That's what it's called now but it had different names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Right. But although you cannot remember the exact title of that institution, was it a civilian or military institution?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Civilian institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the time when you saw him and in your subsequent contacts, and I presume there were on a daily basis, did he wear a military uniform or civilian clothes or what did he wear?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Well, it varied. I remember that I lent him -- that is, I gave him a uniform, because I was issued several uniforms when I came. Military policemen who were there at the time had come earlier, and they gave me their uniforms, as I had none, and I had several separate uniforms, so I gave them to him. So at times, and in Bosnia, it was quite in to -- quite fashionable to wear a combination of military and civilian clothes, that is to wear civilian trousers and a camouflage shirt or the other way around. And I remember well that Mr. Aleksovski had a sweater which on the sleeve had the German flag. Green, a green sweater.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And was that sweater?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: It must have been relief human assistance from Germany so it was donated by humanitarian aid in Germany?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever notice whether such sweaters were the insignia of the German national flag? Did other people wear such sweaters in the territory of Busovaca at the time?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Oh, yes. And even at that time, some policemen asked me, because their sweaters were rather long, some of them asked me to wear it as a dress.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you were also issued such a sweater?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No, no, but a colleague, and it was so long that it looked more like a dress than as a sweater.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujica, awhile ago you said that people used to combine civilian and military clothes. Does this same custom fashion prevail in that territory?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, it is a kind of working clothes, because the quality is rather good in comparison with what now, so it is used for work in the fields and for any kind of hard work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So even today, it's not a rare occurrence that you see an individual sporting some part of military clothes?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujica, did this uniform that Mr. Aleksovski wore, did it have any patches to indicate rank or membership in a unit?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, you mentioned that when you came to Kaonik, you worked for the district military prison in the building. Could you describe that building? What was in that building? What was inside that building? Were they cells or what?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I mean the district military prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: District military prison, there were two offices, one office where the shift leader and the supervisor were, and the second office where -- which was shared by the warden and myself. Those were two office premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, what were your duties? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: When the -- after the warden of the prison district court, I still used the word manager, but I should say warden, and my duty was to keep registry books, that is, to take all the -- take down all the particulars and all the other relevant data, relevant information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I assume, and you will correct me if I'm wrong, that these registries that you kept concerned the detainees at the district military prison; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And those who were disciplined, are they HVO soldiers? Did you keep any records about the persons, the civilians who you said were there when you arrived at Kaonik? Did you keep any records about them?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, I had a computer which I received from the military police, so I entered all the data, the relevant data into the computer, also the data concerning the civilians. And I received the list from the supervisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Ante Jerkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So Ante Jerkovic gave you a list of Muslim civilians who were brought to Kaonik, and you entered the list into the computer?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. Tell us, Mrs. Vujica, where were those people accommodated, I mean, the Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: In the district military court, there were only 16 cells, so it was difficult to accommodate all the civilians there. To my knowledge, some people were also accommodated up there in the hangar, but I haven't seen them, because I had no right of access and communication with people who are detained, and the same applies today, with the exception of women.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. You mentioned a hangar where you said you heard that some people were accommodated. Tell us where the hangar is located in relation to the building in which you worked?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: The same as the prison, but there was some distance, I don't know, of about 100 metres. I can't tell you exactly, but in the same direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. Mrs. Vujica, I will now show you a photograph, and I will ask you to point in that photograph to us and to the Chamber to which building and facilities are you referring to. Can you please show us T1, evidence T1, an aerial photograph of Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I think we should like to have it on the ELMO, please. Could something be done to see it on the ELMO, please? We have it now on the video, this exhibit. Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujica, we now have the picture on the monitor. It is a photograph which is marked down there as Kaonik Camp. Can you recognise the facilities in this photograph and tell us which facilities do you recognise? In the upper part of the photograph, there is a facility marked with the letter "A". What is that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, this is the military police building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is this the building in which military policemen were accommodated?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us whether there is the steel door next to it which is actually the gate into the entire complex?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, and they were guarded by the army or by military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So military police controlled all communication as far as this complex is concerned?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is this the only gate to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think that it would be normal to have more entrances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was this complex surrounded in any way?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, by barbed wire, because it was a former JNA barrack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that Kaonik was a former JNA barrack that was surrounded by barbed wire and that it had just one entrance which is marked by the letter "A"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If you go further by the road, and the picture has been lost for awhile, but now it's back?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: I don't have the picture on my video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So if we continue along the road from the facility marked with the letter "A," tell us what is the next facility marked with the letter "B"?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: It's the district military prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is that the building in which you worked?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you show us what is the building in which you found Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Building "B."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said it's the district military prison, the building with cells?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, the cells in which civilians were located, and I heard that up there there were some more civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you show us on this photograph to which building are you referring when you said "up there"?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: The building up here. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. Tell us, Mrs. Vujica, what are the other facilities within the Kaonik complex? Do you know what was their purpose?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No. It was dangerous because they told me there were a lot of mines that were planted in the area which were not removed, and I didn't go up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. If I understood you correctly, your job -- you worked in the building "B" in the district military prison and practically, you were not allowed to venture around the complex?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, for security reasons too, because the district military prison and the barracks were the target of attacks, because it was near the frontline, and it was frequently shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We no longer need the photograph, and it can be removed from the monitor. Tell us, Mrs. Vujica, when you arrived at Kaonik, you met Mr. Aleksovski, he introduced himself as the warden of the district military prison, and he said that he taught you about your day-to-day duties and showed you how to keep the records. Were the other guards who were at Kaonik, members of the military police, did they have any previous experience for this kind of service in prison facilities?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No, only when Ante Jerkovic arrived who previously worked in a penitentiary, he taught the other guards what to do, the other military policemen, so they received some training from him about the work in the district prisons or the district military prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So only with the arrival of Zlatko Aleksovski, this is when the others received some training. Did you know what kind of experience he had as far as prison work was concerned?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that he worked in the penitentiary in Zenica, and that he was an educator there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mrs. Vujica, can you describe, actually, what kind of duties Aleksovski had in the district military prison? Please tell us first, if you know, of course, who was the person or institution to which Mr. Aleksovski reported as far as the functioning of the district military prison was concerned?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: As far as the work of the district military prison was concerned, he reported to the president of the district military court and the ministry of justice. And the same applies for today. These are the people to whom I report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you said that these were the people to whom he reported, and this is how he communicated with the district military court and its president. Tell us, because of the security for some resources such as food, hygienic material, fuel, spare parts and similar, who was supplying the military prison with that? Which institution?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: The army. We received almost everything from the army, food, clothing, footwear, hygiene. Everything that we used for that purpose, because the army was the only supplier at that time for everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So because of the state of war, the other civilian services did not function?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Only the army?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, only the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you told us before that Zlatko Aleksovski was not a member of the military police, he was not a member of any other military unit, and that on the other hand, the guards at Kaonik were members of the military police?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you, too?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I suppose that you had your own commander in the military police?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was that commander Zlatko Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I mean, in the military sense?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So Zlatko Aleksovski as a warden of the district military prison, what could he do about the guards? I mean, what were his powers vis-à-vis the guards? Could he, for instance, discipline them?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No. Only the commander could do that, the commander of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But, yet, he was in day-to-day communication with these people?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What did he talk with them? What did they talk about?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: You mean the commander of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No. I will repeat my question. So you said that Zlatko Aleksovski was the warden of the district military prison and that the guards came from the military police. He was not the military commander, but he had to train them for their work. It had to be explained what were their duties?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was that his duty?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, that was what he did. He trained the military policemen inside the military prison so that they would know how to treat the detainees, because it was rather difficult to teach them, because it was rather difficult to do that. Because it is not -- it is not the same as if stopping a car on the street, for instance. It is a different kind of duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, he was training the military policemen about their day-to-day jobs as guards of the military prison; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What would happen if some of those military policemen would perform their duties erroneously? What would he do?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: He wouldn't do anything, but the commander of the military police would discipline those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I suppose that the commander would have to be informed about that? Who would inform him about that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: The warden would report about these erroneous duties, and the commander would then discipline them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. Tell us, Mrs. Vujica, did the warden also report about certain events? Did he report to the president of the military court if some incidents occurred or something similar?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will now show you a document and I kindly ask you to comment on it and tell us whether you recognise what you see. I kindly ask now the usher?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D25.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, first of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We still don't have the document. Could we have one? Thank you. Yes, you may continue, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mrs. Vujica, was it your duty to write documents, official letters that were circulated within the prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that you had a computer?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you use it regularly?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, unless there were electricity cuts, and then I used an ordinary typewriter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So we see that this document was written in an ordinary typewriter? Did you write it?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, although it is not visible much, to whom it was addressed?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, to the president of the district court in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And in the bottom, we see that the copy was sent to the president of the district military court?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what was it all about?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: A member of the military police entered the barracks when he wanted to beat a person from Krajina, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Krajisnik, is that a name or a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Krajisnik was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So Zlatko Aleksovski reported the president of the district military court about this?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And tell us the soldier about whom Mr. Aleksovski writes, Vlado Kristo, a soldier. Was he a guard at the prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No, he was, I think, a member of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you, in addition to documents that we just showed you, did you have any opportunity to write similar documents or is this a single such document?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So is that the only such document or did you write similar documents on other occasions?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Like this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, like this one, reporting about the incidents to the district -- to the president of the district court or --

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote such documents at his instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I want this exhibit entered into the evidence under the number D29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Meddegoda, do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I have no objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would now ask the usher to approach the bench so that we can show some other documents to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit for the Defence, D26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I believe there is an error here because Mr. Mikulicic has asked for document 29, but it is 25?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document D25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So we have to make the necessary correction in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, you can continue, Mr. Mikulicic. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and thank you for commenting on the wrong number for the registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujica, before you, you have a document which has been addressed to the president of the district military court in Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The document says that the warden of the district military prison is not able to ensure regular transportation to the court. Can you tell us, what was it all about?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Because of the difficult conditions when the district military prison was set up, we did not have a vehicle of our own, so we were forced to use, when we were supposed to transfer detainees or civilians to the doctor, we did not have -- we could not do that, and we had to borrow a car and we had a car, a Fiat, which did not work so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujica, do you then recognise the signature of this document?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is that Mr. Aleksovski's signature?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The Defence proposes that this document is entered as evidence D26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Meddegoda?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you told us that the conditions in which the district military prison functioned were not very good. You had a shortage of equipment and other resources; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us about the food supplies. Was the food prepared in the prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: The food was prepared in the military police building. There was a cook who prepared the food there, so it was the same food for the guards, for the warden, for the civilian detainees. Everybody ate the same food because there were no conditions to prepare different meals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us about the other resources such as soap, blankets, food, clothes, because it was winter. Did you have enough of those?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No, no, because civilians, when they were visited by the Red Cross, they would bring them some underwear and some clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the Red Cross. Did they visit the prison frequently?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who contacted them? Who spoke to them?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Only the warden of the district prison, Mr. Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did the representatives of the Red Cross bring some materials that they left to you?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, they would leave a document which Mr. Aleksovski would receive, so we would have the origins, the document about the origins.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will show you now some documents, so please tell us what these documents are all about. I now kindly ask the usher to approach so that we can show these documents to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence document D27.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujica, we have before us a document of the Red Cross which says that a delivery was made to the Kaonik prison of soaps and blankets; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature on the bottom of the document?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, Mrs. Beatrice has given these documents and supplies to Mr. Aleksovski, and Mr. Aleksovski signed the receipt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Aleksovski signed this?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened with this materials, were they distributed to the prison or what?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were the soap given to the prisoners and the blankets or did you put them somewhere in store?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, they were given to the prisoners and the civilians, and when they were released, they took them with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujica, I will now show you two more documents of the Red Cross, and I ask -- also kindly ask you to comment on them. Perhaps we can use both documents as one exhibit in order not to lose time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The Defence proposes that these documents, because they are very similar in contents, are registered as Defence material 27A, B and C.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujica, these are also Red Cross documents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So these documents say that, as far as the Kaonik prison is concerned, a supply was made of underwear, training track suits, jackets, boots. Is that what was supplied by the Red Cross to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was it also distributed to detainees and the civilians who were detained there, the Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, and they mostly took it with them, with the exception of blankets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mean when they were released?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, when they were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I suggest that these documents are entered as Exhibits 27B and C, and the first document as 27A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Meddegoda?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence document 27A, B, C. The first document is 27A.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujica, you told us that during your statement that at the beginning of the armed conflict in the Busovaca area, that, actually, ten days after the conflict, you managed to get to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you told us that you learned that in the meantime, Muslim civilians were brought to the Kaonik facility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you, perhaps, know what happened later to the Muslim persons, Muslim civilians, who were brought there? Were they later released and do you know when?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, at the beginning of February, on the 8th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So on the 8th of February, 1993, these people were released from the Kaonik prison; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was at the time when they were released, somebody present from the international organisations?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, John Luc from the Red Cross was present, and when they were released, they had the right to choose where they wanted to go, whether to Zenica, to Merdan, to Kacuni, or to Busovaca, so it was their choice where they wanted to go. I was surprised, for instance, that there was a bus of them -- a bus load which took them to Busovaca, and I know two brothers who returned because they were friends of my brother. And their names are Miralem and Salem Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Those persons, those civilians, when they were released in the presence of the international Red Cross could state their preference as to their point of destination, and you know that a number of them, after being released from Kaonik, stated that they wanted to come back to Busovaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did some civilian prisoners, Muslims, stay behind in Kaonik after that? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us proceed now. The situation begins to calm down, armed conflicts also begin to calm down, roads become more possible and the life goes back to normal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, the second conflict breaks out. When is that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: In the middle of April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were you faced with the same situation as during the first armed conflict, that is, could you go to work or not?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No, I could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So how long did it take before you could really go to work?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: I wouldn't know exactly, perhaps five or six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you came back to work, did you find Muslim civilians in Kaonik again?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you know who had brought those persons to Kaonik? Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Mostly the military police, the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever think why those people had been brought to Kaonik? Did you ever discuss it and do you have your own news about that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Well, as I stayed back at home to be with my child, so it is, I guess, more than likely that they also wanted to find some shelter, and the prison was the only possibility where they could find shelter and stay alive because, you know, in view of the building materials, the walls there were made of very good material, very solid material, and they could withstand the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And was there the shelling of Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if anyone was wounded during the shelling?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you, perhaps, remember if any of the prisoners or those civilians was ever wounded at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if any of the guards was ever wounded, the security?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, in the second conflict, the security service, that is, the military policemen were posted to the defence line, and they were guarding the -- and the prison was guarded by the Domobrans then, and three or four were wounded. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But no prisoner?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In that second conflict, did those Muslim civilians accommodated in that hangar, as during the first conflict, or somewhere else? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: I don't know about the second hangar. I know they were in the district military prison. About up there, I did not go up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujica, do you know anything if those persons who were accommodated in Kaonik, and I mean Muslim civilians, did they have any labour obligations that they had to comply with?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Labour obligations?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, were those persons taken out of the prison Kaonik to perform certain duties?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No, those civilians, those prisoners didn't do anything outside, except, perhaps, to go and fetch food, bring food, and one had to do it because the canteen was below that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We're talking about these detainees, but there's something else I should like to know, Mrs. Vujica. What I should like to know is whether you know if those Muslims, if those civilians, that you find there came there after the first or second conflict, whether they were taking out of Kaonik to do some digging or some other works?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, some commanders from the frontline ordered them to go and dig the trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you saw that they were being taken out of Kaonik. Who came to fetch them?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Largely, the military, but I don't know very many of those soldiers, but I think it was the military police, by and large.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, if the population were not at Kaonik but who had stayed behind at home, did they also have to perform those duties, that is, were they also under labour obligations?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, even my father had to go to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your father too?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How old was your father?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: He was 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And he was not a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Not at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And yet he was under obligation to go and dig?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, it was a kind of a labour obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember as to how was he notified that he had to go and dig? Would somebody come to fetch them or what?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Well, usually the military police came or they would get a request or some such document that they would have to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But there were occasions when the military police would come after him, and then he would go to the place where he had to work; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know if it happened once or several times?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Several times. Once it was at 2.00. I remember mother telling me that they woke him up at 2.00 and he had to go.

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, probably because of the safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And do you know where did he go to dig trenches? Do you know in what part of the municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: The first time he was on Strane and then he was sent elsewhere, and later on, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know if other men in your village were also under labour obligation?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, there were some young men who were not members of the army and they were also taken to dig. I remember my neighbour, my former neighbour, Andjelko Vujica, and his brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: They also went to dig?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, together with my father.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujica, you mentioned that in April, when the conflicts were at their most, the guards from the prison were taken to the frontline, and that under the circumstances, there were guards who were brought in to guard the prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujica, could you tell us something about the security situation in the area of Busovaca? You already said something about it. You said that some shells hit the Kaonik facility itself. You said that could not come to work regularly at the time when conflicts would gain momentum because it was impossible to pass through. But do you know if shells fell on the town of Busovaca and surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujica, what do you think, was there a place in the municipality of Busovaca which would be safe from shells?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No, at that time, there was no safe place. I was unsafe at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But you said you stayed at home because of your child?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you also said that the structures at Kaonik were rather solid, and that although Kaonik was shelled, none of the prisoners were wounded?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know if any of those civilians, Muslims or prisoners, detainees at the district prison, did anyone fall ill seriously or contract an infectious disease or some infection or something? Do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No. To this day, no detainee, that is, no civilian has ever fallen ill or suffered from any contagious disease nor has there been any infection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know if any representatives of the medical centres came to those premises?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, when we had some transportation, then we would take them up there, and when not, then they would come to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What were the hygiene conditions, that is, I mean, lavatories, toilets, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Bad, very bad. There were only two WCs, one for the personnel, and the other for persons who were there in prison. So they sometimes used our WC.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you know if persons who were there, if they could use the WC depending on the circumstances or were they prohibited from doing that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No, they were not prohibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujica, tell us, what was the situation with fumigation, with rodent extermination? Did you have any means to do it?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: What we got from the army, from the Red Cross, we used it, but it was very bad. We were in a very poor situation, and we did not have enough of that but it was all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was what I was going to ask you, Mrs. Vujica. Did the situation in Kaonik differ from the situation throughout the municipality of Busovaca or did you share the same lot?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: We all shared the same lot. We all were in the same situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you know, and that is my next question, when doctors from the medical centre in Busovaca, when doctors would prescribe house care or requested that they be spared for work, were these recommendations or advice of the doctors heeded to? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujica, in the beginning of your testimony, you said that you still worked at the same facility. If you now compare it, the conditions today with the conditions of 1993, what would you say? Has something been added? Has some new structures been built? Tell us something about that.

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: The district prison in Busovaca is not different much from the district prison at the time of war. There are some slight changes. Two WCs had been built, or rather, a WC, with a lavatory, with a bathroom, that is now supporting convicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So to this day, on the premises of that same district military prison which at present is called district prison, convicts use the WC in the passage way, the same way as they did during the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know if an international inspection came to inspect the conditions there?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, in the beginning of 1993, we had the visit of some international commission which inspected the prison, which talked to detainees and convicts and talked to representatives of the district prison and looked into documentation and they noted their satisfaction with the conditions of work and life there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujica, will you please repeat when was this inspection? Was it the beginning of 1993 as the transcript says?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So it was 1998. And they had no particular objections to the conditions in the prison; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And is it true that the accommodations in the prison today are not much different from the conditions in the same prison in 1993?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No, there are slight changes. For instance, we have the light bulbs in the cells now, and formerly, they were affixed to the bars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We have no further questions, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Right. I think it will be a very good time to make a break and we shall go into recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mrs. Blazenka Vujica, Mr. Mikulicic, we must always remember, as you know, that between you, there is always an interpreter, and this morning things were slightly complicated. So I should like to ask Mrs. Blazenka Vujica to speak slower, to make some break so that the interpreters could follow because, unfortunately, we do not speak your language. Will you please take note of this? Thank you very much. Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor, and you may continue -- oh, no, no, you have already concluded. Mr. Meddegoda, I believe it is now your turn to continue. Mr. Meddegoda?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have a few questions for this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Vujica.

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you questions on behalf of the Prosecution, and I hope you will be able to assist me to the best of your ability and to the best of your recollection. Now, your evidence this morning was that you joined the military police of the HVO in mid December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: I was mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Correct, yes. And having been mobilised, you were sent to the Kaonik -- you were mobilised as a military policewoman. And for the reason that there were no women prisoners to be looked after, you were assigned to the Kaonik prison; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: I was transferred. I was a member of the military police. I was a member of the military police within the district prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So even within the district prison, your evidence is that you continued to be a member of the military police when you functioned as secretary to the warden of the prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Prior to that, apart from your work in your uncle's store, prior to that, did you work as a secretary to any other organisation or to a company?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you have any previous secretarial experience before being transferred to Kaonik as secretary?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you, at any point in time, function as secretary to the Security and Intelligence Service of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You're certain that you never functioned as secretary of the Security and Intelligence Service of the HVO headed by Anto Sliskovic (phoen)?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: As the administrative secretary, you said when you came to the camp -- after coming to the camp, it was in early February that you met Mr. Aleksovski for the first time?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And that was about the 5th or the 6th of February of 1993?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: I did not say that. I never mentioned the 5th or 6th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujica, when did you first report to work at the Kaonik prison camp?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: I was mobilised for the military police, and I started working at the military police in the middle of December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And you worked in the Kaonik prison facility, as you said in your evidence this morning, until the first conflict broke out on January 25th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: From the very beginning, I worked at the district military prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When did the conflict break out for the first time in the Busovaca area in 1993?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: On the 25th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: As a result of that, I take it it was your evidence that you did not come to work -- you could not come to work for about ten days from the 25th of February?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So that would mean that you came back to work after the conflict broke out on about the 5th or 6th of February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And it was then that you met for the first time Mr. Aleksovski as warden of the prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you. It was also your evidence this morning that when you came on the 5th or the 6th of February, that was about ten days after the first conflict broke out, you found a lot of Muslim civilians detained within the buildings of the prison facility?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you remember about how many Muslim civilians were detained in that facility when you first saw them around the 5th or the 6th of February?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Where did you see them detained? In which buildings of the facility did you see them detained?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: In the district military prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: About how many did you see in the district military prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: As I said, I can't remember exactly how many of them were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you give us an approximate figure of how many prisoners were there, how many Muslim civilians were there the day you saw them for the first time?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No, no, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You also said that it was on the 8th of February that those prisoners were released from the prison facility?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: That was only a day after you first saw them?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Vujica, could you please help us, where was your office when you started working as secretary in the Kaonik military prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: In the district military prison building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask the usher please to show to the witness document D1, a Defence document which was shown to the witness a while ago, Your Honours. Your Honours, the picture has disappeared from the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: It is already on the ELMO. It should be on the video too. Press "Video."

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: There we are. Now it appears on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And your evidence is that that is the building that is marked "B" on the exhibit that is on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Was your office in that building from the very first day that you reported for duty?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: To the military police, no. I first was assigned to the building marked "A" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: -- when I arrived in the middle of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And that's the building you said which is at the entrance gate which is the building that is marked "A"?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Where in that building was your office located?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: In which building, "A" or "B"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I'm asking you where in that building, where in building "A," was your office located?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: In the building marked "A." When I already started working in the military police, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Okay. I'll take you step by step to that building. Now, what type of building was building "A"? Could you describe the building?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Well, you heard earlier, probably there were dormitories there. I don't know. The JNA used it before. I don't know what it was used for before because I never came there before that. And nobody had access there but the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When you had access to it after the JNA, after the HVO took over that complex, can you tell this court -- could you describe that building to the court? Was it a building similar to the building "B" that you've marked already on the document D1, on the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No, they were different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How was it different to that building, to building "B"?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Building "B" was a hangar that was refurbished and cells were made. And building "A" earlier had some offices, and I think that's the difference, and it had a floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: On which floor was your office, the office in which you worked?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: The ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know what else was there in building "A"? What other offices were located in building "A"?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: A kitchen and dormitories for the HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were the HVO soldiers present at the time you were assigned to -- when you started working in building "A"?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I take it that those military policemen were all dressed in the uniform of the military police or in military uniform?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't need the exhibit anymore. It may be taken off the ELMO, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, as part of your secretarial functions, it was your evidence that you had to prepare the lists of -- in addition to other functions, you also had to prepare the list of prisoners who were detained within the buildings of the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: The list of detainees and civilians who were there I made at the instructions of the security chief or at the instructions of the warden.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I take it that the list consisted of all the detainees and the civilians who were within the district military prison building and the hangar building which was adjoining the district military prison building?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And whenever prisoners and civilians were brought either to the district military prison building or to the hangar building adjoining that, you prepared such lists on the instructions of the warden of the prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Was there any other secretary who was charged with preparing lists of prisoners, lists of civilians and detainees, who were within the prison facility?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No, I was the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were there any other officials in the camp who prepared such lists, for instance, the commanders, the guards, the shift commanders or people like that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: The shift commanders were not allowed to make any instructions of their own. They had to receive instructions from the warden. Well, of course, only in the situations when the warden was absent they had such powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether in the absence -- do you know, because you worked with the warden as secretary in the same office, do you know in the absence of the warden, whether such lists were prepared by the shift commanders or by the guards?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Only when they were taken for labour duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you tell us the procedure, how these lists are prepared when they were taken for labour duty? Could you please tell this court what the procedure was, how the lists are prepared by the shift commanders or by the guards when the prisoners are taken for labour duty?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: I don't know. I guess they would just take some order or sequence. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So I take it that you were the only secretary that was assigned to the camp, to the prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, a policewoman and a secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: All right. And you were present when prisoners were taken for labour duty?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Not always. I was not there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: But at times, there were sometimes when you were present when prisoners were taken for duty, though not always?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How were they taken?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: At the request of some commanders of the frontline, they would request a number of people, and then the security chief would make a list. And according to that list, they were sent there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And they would be taken by the commanders who would come and request for those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Not the commanders, they wouldn't come. They would request. But military policemen would come and take the people away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And it is at the time that they are taken away that a list is prepared?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your evidence is that no list is prepared before that. It is only at the time that the prisoners are being taken away that a list is prepared?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Before the prisoners would be taken, the list would be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who would make that -- sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: When a policeman would arrive with a request for a certain number of people to be taken away for trench digging, the supervisor of the security service would make a list containing the names of people who would be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And such lists would be made on the instructions of the warden of the prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the supervisor was in charge of that exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I understand that, but no list would be prepared unless there were instructions from the warden of the prison to prepare such a list?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: No, the warden was not there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: At the time when the warden was there, the warden would give such instructions, and then the list would be prepared?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: It was a routine procedure, so we knew that the supervisor would have to do that. And the warden sometimes had nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Yes, Mrs. Vujica, I know about the warden. But at times, the warden was present in the camp, as you said before. No lists were prepared unless on the instructions of the warden of the camp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in consultation with the supervisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said in the course of your evidence this morning that another group of Bosniaks were brought to the Kaonik prison sometime in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: BLAZENKA VUJICA
utterances.text: Yes.
